column2: Respiratory sinus arrhythmia (rate rises on inspiration, falls on expiration) is normal, especially in the young; all beats are sinus, so reassure.
2:1 block with narrow QRS in a sleeping young athlete is almost certainly vagally mediated AV-nodal block; infranodal block usually has broad QRS.
Atropine removes vagal tone at SA and AV nodes, raising the rate and restoring 1:1 conduction in nodal block; in infranodal block it may worsen the ratio.
Parkinsonian tremor artefact (4–6 Hz) can mimic flutter, AF or VT; regular QRS complexes seen through it confirm sinus rhythm, so no treatment.
Saw-tooth waves in II, III, aVF with 2:1 conduction is typical flutter; its stroke risk equals AF, and CHA2DS2-VASc is high, so anticoagulate before ablation.
A negative delta wave and LBBB-like QRS in V1 indicate a right-sided accessory pathway; a positive delta in V1 indicates a left-sided pathway.
A wide ventricular rhythm at 75/min soon after successful lysis in a well patient is accelerated idioventricular rhythm: observe. Suppression is harmful.
Sinus pauses with absent P waves plus bradycardia in an older person is sick sinus syndrome. In AV block P waves are present but not conducted.
If vagal manoeuvres fail, adenosine (6 mg rapid bolus, then 12 and 18 mg) terminates AV-node-dependent SVT; verapamil if asthmatic.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: after vagal manoeuvres give adenosine, which ends AVNRT/AVRT or unmasks flutter waves. Cardiovert only if adverse features.
PR > 200 ms with every P conducted is first-degree AV block (ageing, vagal tone, AV-nodal drugs, inferior MI); no treatment needed alone.
Dropped P waves with a fixed PR in conducted beats is Mobitz II: infranodal, can progress abruptly to complete block, so pace permanently.
Atrial rate 300/min with ventricular rate 150/min is atrial flutter with 2:1 block; suspect it in any regular narrow tachycardia near 150/min.
Synchronised DC cardioversion restores sinus rhythm in > 90% of flutter (drugs work poorly); anticoagulate as for AF. CTI ablation prevents recurrence.
Paroxysmal palpitations with sweating: check TFTs, metanephrines (phaeochromocytoma), ambulatory ECG and echo. An upper GI study has no role.
Irregular tachycardia without P waves is AF; first-line rate control in a stable patient is a beta-blocker (bisoprolol). Flecainide is for rhythm control.
Stable regular narrow-complex tachycardia: vagal manoeuvres first (carotid massage if young, no bruit); then adenosine, or verapamil if asthmatic.
Syncope during exercise is a cardiac red flag (HCM, long QT, WPW, Brugada, ARVC); a 12-lead ECG is the essential first test.
Brief self-terminating AF with CHA2DS2-VASc 0 and a normal heart needs no anticoagulation; antiplatelets are never used for AF stroke prevention.
CHA2DS2-VASc 5: oral anticoagulation. After ACS with AF: brief triple therapy (≤ 1 week), then DOAC + clopidogrel to 12 months, then DOAC alone.
Weight loss, fatigue and new AF in a young woman suggest hyperthyroidism: check TSH and free T4 (recommended in all new AF).
AF < 48 h can be cardioverted once heparin is started. Prior MI contraindicates flecainide, so use DC cardioversion (or amiodarone).
Infrequent paroxysmal AF in a normal heart: 'pill-in-the-pocket' flecainide with an AV-nodal blocker. Sotalol is contraindicated in asthma.
The a wave is atrial contraction, so it is absent in AF. Cannon a waves = AV dissociation; large v waves = tricuspid regurgitation.
Rapid SVT ending in a long pause with dizziness/syncope is tachy–brady sick sinus syndrome: permanent pacemaker, then rate-control drugs safely.
Ischaemic stroke with AF (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 6): lifelong anticoagulation, DOAC preferred (or warfarin INR 2–3), started within days depending on infarct size.
Flutter waves ~250/min with 2:1 block in a stable patient: rate control first with IV metoprolol, then anticoagulation and elective cardioversion/ablation.
Progressive PR lengthening until a dropped beat is Mobitz I (AV-nodal, benign): observe and review AV-nodal drugs if asymptomatic.
Complete heart block after anterior MI is infranodal with an unreliable escape rhythm: pace (temporary, then assess permanent) even if BP is stable.
Regular saw-tooth waves ~300/min with a QRS after every fourth is atrial flutter with 4:1 block; decongestants and lung disease are triggers.
Older patient with dilated LA, now rate-controlled and asymptomatic: continue rate control plus long-term anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc ≥ 3).
Short PR, delta wave and wide QRS is pre-excitation (WPW); palpitations or syncope warrant an EP study and pathway ablation.
Congenital long QT is most often loss of potassium-channel function (KCNQ1 LQT1, hERG LQT2); treat with nadolol/propranolol and avoid QT drugs.
AF lasting > 7 days (or needing cardioversion after 7 days) is persistent; paroxysmal ends within 7 days, permanent means rhythm control abandoned.
In complete heart block the varying AV interval makes S1 intensity vary (with intermittent cannon a waves). Stop bisoprolol and pace.
Bradycardia with an adverse feature (syncope): IV atropine 500 µg, repeat to 3 mg; then transcutaneous pacing or isoprenaline/adrenaline infusion.
CHA2DS2-VASc 5 (age 75 = 2, female, prior TIA = 2): anticoagulate (DOAC); AF during acute illness often recurs. Aspirin is not used.
Adenosine is given 6 mg, then 12 mg, then 18 mg by rapid bolus with flush; repeating 6 mg rarely works. Verapamil if adenosine fails.
LBBB occurs with IHD, hypertension/LVH, AS, cardiomyopathy and conduction fibrosis. Secundum ASD causes RBBB with right axis deviation.
QTc 500 ms is prolonged (high torsades risk); hypokalaemia (flat T, U waves) is a common cause. Hypercalcaemia and digoxin shorten the QT.
Torsades needs a long QT: TCAs, SAH, hypothermia, congenital LQTS, low K/Mg/Ca. Hypercalcaemia shortens the QT. Treat with IV magnesium 2 g.
AF with HFrEF and brittle asthma: rate-limiting CCBs are negatively inotropic and beta-blockers are precluded, so digoxin is used.
CHB after inferior MI is nodal (narrow escape, atropine-responsive, usually resolves), so pacing is not needed if stable; after anterior MI it is.
Penicillin-sensitive streptococcal native-valve IE: IV benzylpenicillin 4 weeks (or 2 weeks with gentamicin if uncomplicated). Vancomycin is for allergy.
Symptomatic severe AS (area < 1 cm², mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg) with EF < 50% needs AVR — surgical or TAVI by heart team. No drug improves outlook.
